title: Entropy production of active matter systems as indicator for computing performance
authors: Patrick Egenlauf, Hannes A. Kröninger, Arnulf Kung, Mario U. Gaimann, Miriam Klopotek
abstract: Physical systems can process information through their natural dynamics, offering alternatives to conventional digital computing. Reservoir computing offers a basic framework by using a nonlinear substrate to map inputs into rich dynamical states read out by a simple linear layer. Active matter substrates are striking examples; they continuously consume energy and produce entropy. Theoretically, entropy production (EP) can describe the irreversibility and distance from equilibrium. But it remains unclear whether it can track computational capabilities. We address this conceptual gap by analyzing a driven swarm reservoir model. The system EP is computed from phase-space contraction and the bath EP from heat flow, separately, and put in direct association to prediction performance on a Lorenz-63 task. Via force parameter scans, we show that dynamical regimes with the strongest response to a driver as well as dissipation coincide with peak performance. Therein, the dynamical discrepancy between innate (minimal dissipation) and driven transferred heat (maximal dissipation) is sharpest. Generally, driver work and relative differences of driven and undriven EP closely mirror the performance landscape. The system EP, derived from a generalized Liouville-equation estimator, and heat flow provide complementary diagnostics and metrics, which are most robust in the best-performing regime. These results extend prior expectations that dissipation matters for computation by identifying when and how it becomes predictive. They also relate inference power to innate dynamics, pointing to generic principles for physical computing and where EP offers a screening metric for reservoirs and other base substrates.
summary: This paper investigates if entropy production can predict the computational power of active matter systems. By analyzing a driven swarm model, the authors find that peak performance coincides with specific regimes characterized by strong dissipation and predictable thermodynamic responses. The work establishes EP as a potentially robust, task-agnostic metric for assessing physical computing substrates.
main_problem: The study addresses whether entropy production (EP), a measure of thermodynamic irreversibility, can serve as a predictive indicator for the computational performance of physical systems.
main_result: Dynamical regimes exhibiting peak computational performance correlate strongly with those showing strong dissipation and robust thermodynamic responses. Driver work and relative differences in EP closely mirror the system's performance landscape.
method: The authors calculate system entropy production (from phase-space contraction) and bath entropy production (from heat flow) for a driven active matter model, correlating these metrics against prediction accuracy on tasks like Lorenz-63.
model_or_system: The research uses a driven swarm reservoir model of active matter, governed by non-Hamiltonian Newtonian equations of motion. The system is analyzed across various driving forces and parameter scans to test the thermodynamic link to computation.
key_observables: Entropy Production (System EP, Bath EP), Prediction Performance (on Lorenz-63 task), Driver Work, Dissipation levels.
important_parameters: Force parameters, dissipation strength, coupling between innate dynamics and driven heat transfer.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on calculating $\dot{S}_{sys}$ via Gibbs entropy and $\dot{S}_{bath}$ from heat flow ($\dot{Q}/T$), despite acknowledging potential inconsistencies with full thermodynamic closure for the non-Hamiltonian system.
figures_summary: Not specified, but the notes mention correlation tables (Table V & VI) summarizing Pearson and Spearman correlations between performance metrics and various thermodynamic quantities across different attractors.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the conceptual gap between EP and computation, details the calculation of $\dot{S}_{sys}$ and $\dot{S}_{bath}$ for the active matter model, and then systematically compares these derived thermodynamic diagnostics against measured computational performance metrics via parameter scans and correlation analysis.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete framework for using non-equilibrium thermodynamics (like EP) as a diagnostic tool to characterize information processing capacity in complex physical systems, which has implications for understanding energy efficiency in computation beyond standard quantum models.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: Representative snapshot of the swarm reservoir setup. Blue dots are agents (n = 200), the red dot is the predator (input) and green circles show Gaussian readout kernels (centers cm and widths σm). The linear readout is trained to predict the predator position at t + ∆t (pink star).

FIG. 2: Time series of the system entropy rate and heat flow for the undriven and driven system for different regimes (see Tab. II). For the undriven system, the first 104 steps are not discarded as burn-in to show the relaxation dynamics. Only the first two steps are removed to avoid the initial condition biasing the plot. The solid lines represent the mean EP rate over the different seeds, hence different initial conditions, and the shaded regions represent the standard deviation. The system entropy is negative for all three regimes. The difference in the dynamics of the three regimes is clearly visible in the system entropy rate and the heat flow.

FIG. 3: System entropy and transferred heat for the undriven system across the parameter scan of the speed controller force (Eq. (10d)) and the corresponding coefficient of variation. Gray areas indicate crashed simulations due to extreme parameter configurations. The system entropy is negative for all parameter configurations except one, hence the color bar indicates the absolute value of the system entropy.

FIG. 4: System entropy and transferred heat for the driven system across the parameter scan of the speed controller force (Eq. (10d)) and the corresponding coefficient of variation. Gray areas indicate crashed simulations due to extreme parameter configurations. The system entropy is negative for all parameter configurations, hence the color bar indicates the negative of the system entropy.

FIG. 5: Relative difference between the driven and undriven case for the (a) system entropy and (b) transferred heat across the parameter scan of the speed controller force (Eq. (10d)). Gray areas indicate crashed simulations due to extreme parameter configurations.
